Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle describes a fundamental limit in quantum mechanics: you cannot simultaneously know both the exact position and the exact momentum of a particle. The more precisely you measure one, the less precisely you can know the other.

To understand this without oversimplifying, consider the analogy of trying to take a high-speed photograph of a speeding car at night. If you use a very fast shutter speed to freeze the car’s position clearly, the image of the headlights becomes a sharp dot, but you lose information about how fast it was moving because the light didn’t have time to streak. Conversely, if you use a slow shutter speed to capture the streak of light (showing speed and direction), the car’s exact position becomes blurred and uncertain. The act of measuring one property inherently disturbs or obscures the other. This is not due to faulty equipment, but a fundamental property of wave-particle duality in quantum systems.

The name of the planet humans live on is Earth.
